core: Metaphysics as inquiry into general features of reality
Ontology and questions of existence and categories
Identity, persistence, change, and material constitution
supporting: The historical origin of the title metaphysics
The distinction from empirical physics and supernatural speculation
outOfScope: A history of every metaphysical tradition
Detailed theories of personal identity, mind-body relations, free will, or time

claims.claim: Metaphysics investigates broad questions about reality, including being, categories, causation, space and time, persistence, modality, mind and body, and freedom and determinism.
Ontology is a part of metaphysics concerned with what exists and with the most general features and relations of the entities included in an account of reality.
Metaphysical problems include questions about categories of being, substance, modality, space and time, persistence and constitution, causation, and the mental and physical.
The contemporary scope of metaphysics is broader than historical descriptions focused only on being as such, first causes, or unchanging things, and its boundaries are contested.

The label metaphysics does not mean an inquiry that simply goes beyond physics; the term originates in the placement of Aristotle's treatise after works on nature, while current metaphysical inquiry includes problems connected to empirical disciplines.
Philosophers differ about metaphysics's proper methodology and even whether it is possible as an enterprise, so the lesson presents its questions rather than a final inventory of reality.

conflictingEvidence.issue: How to define metaphysics and whether its various problems share one defining feature.
positions: Historical accounts emphasize being as such, first causes, or unchanging things.
Contemporary use includes a wider range of problems such as modality, persistence, causation, and mind-body relations.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson uses a broad, current introductory description and explicitly notes the field's contested boundaries rather than treating one historical definition as exhaustive.
